questions.stem: A payments team in a monorepo keeps its card-data handling rules in `services/payments/CLAUDE.md`. Engineers launch Claude Code from the repository root. When they ask Claude to change an existing file under `services/payments/`, the rules are followed. When they ask it to create a new module there from a spec, the rules are ignored, and `/context` in such a session shows the file missing from **Memory files**. The team wants the rules applied in every session for every engineer, with as little restructuring as possible. What should they do?

options.text: Convert the file into a path-scoped rule at `.claude/rules/payments.md` whose `paths` frontmatter lists `services/payments/**`, so the rules attach to every file under that directory.
Have each engineer copy the rules into `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, because user-scope memory loads in every session no matter which directory Claude Code starts from.
Import the file from the root `CLAUDE.md` with an `@services/payments/CLAUDE.md` line, or move the must-follow rules there, so they load at launch rather than on demand.
Rewrite the rules with a prominent **MUST** header and have engineers begin each session by asking Claude to confirm it has read the payments rules.

questions.explanation: `CLAUDE.md` files in the launch directory and its ancestors load at launch. A `CLAUDE.md` in a subdirectory loads on demand, when Claude reads a file in that directory with the Read tool. It does not load at startup, and not when Claude writes or creates files there. That explains the symptom: editing an existing file triggers a read, creating a new module does not. Anything that must apply to every session belongs in a file that loads at launch. Importing the subdirectory file from the root `CLAUDE.md` with `@path` keeps the rules where the team maintains them, and the committed root file reaches every engineer.

whyWrong.A: Path-scoped rules load when Claude reads files matching the glob, not on every tool use. Creating a new file under `services/payments/` still wouldn't load them, so the symptom stays.
whyWrong.B: User-scope memory lives on one laptop and isn't version controlled, so the rules drift between engineers and never reach new hires. Shared project rules belong in the repository.
whyWrong.D: Wording can't help a file that was never loaded. `/context` already showed the file was absent, so this is a prompt-only fix for a loading problem.

questions.mindset: When an instruction is ignored, first ask whether it ever reached the model, then where it loads from.

questions.stem: One engineer says Claude Code behaves strangely in a shared repository. Some shell commands are refused for no visible reason, and files are reformatted after every edit. Five teammates in the same repository and branch see none of this. The engineer has collected personal hooks, plugins and MCP servers over months. The platform lead wants to find the cause with as little guesswork as possible. What should the engineer do FIRST?

options.text: Start with `claude --safe-mode`. If the problem disappears, re-enable customizations one at a time; if it persists, retest with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` pointed at an empty directory.
Uninstall and reinstall Claude Code, since a corrupted or outdated installation is the most common reason one machine behaves differently from teammates on the same repository.
In the affected session, ask Claude to review its own configuration and explain why it is refusing commands and reformatting files, then apply its suggestions.
Replace the engineer's whole `~/.claude` directory with a copy from a teammate whose setup works, so both machines start from the same configuration.

questions.explanation: The problem affects one person on a shared repository, which points to their personal configuration. `--safe-mode` turns off CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers and custom commands and agents, but keeps authentication, built-in tools and permissions. If the symptom goes away, a customization is the cause, and adding them back one by one finds it. If the symptom stays, a session with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` pointed at an empty directory and launched outside the repo rules out everything under `~/.claude`. Managed settings still apply in both tests.

whyWrong.B: Reinstalling doesn't touch `~/.claude` or project settings, so the configuration that causes the problem stays. It also tells you nothing about the cause.
whyWrong.C: Asking the model to diagnose itself in the affected session depends on the same configuration that may be at fault. It's guesswork, not isolation.
whyWrong.D: Overwriting the directory throws away the engineer's settings and credentials and still doesn't say which item caused the problem, so it can come back.

questions.mindset: Isolate before you fix: switch customizations off, confirm the symptom changes, then bisect.

questions.stem: A team commits a `.mcp.json` at the repository root. It defines a local stdio MCP server with `"command": "node"` and `"args": ["./tools/mcp/server.js"]`. Engineers who start Claude Code from the repository root get the server's tools. Engineers who start it from `services/billing/` see the server marked failed in `/mcp`. Credentials are not involved. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Move `.mcp.json` into the `.claude/` folder so Claude Code finds it no matter which subdirectory the engineer starts the session from.
Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md telling Claude to change to the repository root before it uses any of the MCP server's tools.
Ask affected engineers to re-approve the project server in `/mcp`, because approval is stored per directory and has to be granted again in each one.
Change the server entry so it doesn't depend on the launch directory, for example by using an absolute path to the script or an executable on `PATH`.

questions.explanation: Relative paths in an MCP server's `command` or `args` resolve against the directory Claude Code was started from, not the location of `.mcp.json`. So `./tools/mcp/server.js` exists only when the session starts at the repo root. The documented fix is an absolute path for local scripts. Executables on `PATH`, such as `npx` or `uvx`, work as they are.

whyWrong.A: Project MCP config belongs at the repository root as `.mcp.json`. A file inside `.claude/` doesn't load, so this would break the server for everyone.
whyWrong.B: Claude can't change how a stdio server process is launched. The server fails to start before any tool call, so an instruction can't help.
whyWrong.C: An unapproved server shows as waiting for approval, not failed. The symptom depends on the launch directory, which points to path resolution.

questions.mindset: When a failure depends on where you start from, suspect relative-path resolution before blaming auth or the model.

questions.stem: After an internal docs MCP server is upgraded, `/mcp` shows it as **connected**, but with zero tools. Claude now answers documentation questions from general knowledge. The server's owner says the new version starts cleanly on her machine. An engineer wants the quickest path to the real cause. Which approach is MOST effective?

options.text: Rewrite the server's tool descriptions to be more specific, so Claude prefers them over its general knowledge whenever someone asks a documentation question.
Choose **Reconnect** in `/mcp`. If the tool count stays at zero, run `claude --debug=mcp` and read the server's stderr in the session's debug log.
Remove the server and add it again with `claude mcp add --scope user`, because a user-scoped server is more likely than a project one to keep its tools.
Add a CLAUDE.md rule that tells Claude it must always use the docs server for documentation questions and never answer from its general knowledge.

questions.explanation: A server that is connected but lists zero tools started up but isn't returning a tool list. Claude can't call tools it was never given. The documented steps are to reconnect from `/mcp` first and, if the count stays at zero, run `claude --debug=mcp` and read the server's stderr in `~/.claude/debug/<session-id>.txt`. That shows what the upgraded server is doing differently in this environment.

whyWrong.A: Descriptions only help Claude choose among tools it already has. Here there are none to choose from.
whyWrong.C: Scope controls where the configuration lives and who gets it. It doesn't change whether the server returns a tool list, so the fault would follow the server.
whyWrong.D: An instruction can't make tools appear. This is a prompt-only fix for a problem in the server's integration.

questions.mindset: Read the server's own output first: logs come before prompt tweaks.

questions.stem: A repository's committed settings include the deny rule `Bash(rm *)` so that Claude Code can never delete files from the shell. A post-incident review finds that Claude removed a directory of build artifacts with `find ./out -name '*.o' -delete`, and in another session with `/bin/rm -r`. The security lead wants deletions to be reliably prevented, with as little ongoing maintenance as possible. What should the team do?

options.text: Block deletions with a PreToolUse hook that inspects each Bash command, adding the sandbox as an OS-level layer, instead of relying on a command-string deny pattern.
Add a deny rule for each variant found so far, such as `Bash(find *-delete*)` and `Bash(/bin/rm *)`, and keep extending the list whenever a review turns up a new one.
Add a prominent CLAUDE.md rule saying that Claude must never delete files by any method, and that it should ask a human to run every deletion.
Switch the team's default permission mode to `plan`, since plan mode stops Claude from changing anything until a person approves the plan.

questions.explanation: Bash permission rules match the command text Claude writes, not the program that actually runs. So `Bash(rm *)` doesn't catch `/bin/rm`, `find -delete`, `bash -c 'rm ...'`, or a script that deletes files. The docs say a deny rule covers the usual spelling and is not a security boundary around the program; for a hard guarantee, use a PreToolUse hook that applies your own logic to the full command, or the sandbox for OS-level filesystem limits. A hook that exits 2 blocks the call before permission rules are evaluated, and the sandbox restricts where shell commands and their child processes can write regardless of how a command is spelled.

whyWrong.B: Listing patterns is never finished. There are endless ways to delete a file (`xargs rm`, `python -c`, `unlink`), so each new review finds another gap.
whyWrong.C: CLAUDE.md is guidance, not enforcement. The docs say to use permissions or hooks for anything that must never happen.
whyWrong.D: Plan mode blocks edits until a plan is approved, but approved shell commands can still run during planning, and the restriction ends once the plan is approved. It doesn't stop deletions.

questions.mindset: String matching is not a security boundary. Enforce at the action, not the spelling.

questions.stem: An internal agent built on the Messages API keeps its own conversation history. To save tokens, it keeps only `text` and `tool_use` blocks from each assistant response before appending it to the history. Since the team turned thinking on, every request that sends a `tool_result` back fails with a 400 `invalid_request_error` saying thinking blocks in the latest assistant message cannot be modified. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Turn thinking off on every request that carries a `tool_result`, and turn it back on for the first request of each new user turn so reasoning still happens.
Add automatic retries with exponential backoff to the request wrapper, since 400 errors during multi-step tool use are usually short-lived.
Strip thinking blocks from every assistant turn in the history, not just the latest one, so the conversation is consistent and the API accepts it.
Pass the latest assistant message back exactly as received, keeping its `thinking` and `redacted_thinking` blocks, and filter only where the docs allow it.

questions.explanation: Within a tool-use turn, every `thinking` and `redacted_thinking` block from the latest assistant message must be passed back exactly as received, including blocks whose `thinking` field is empty. Filtering content blocks by type is the documented cause of this 400. The fix is in the application's history handling: pass the assistant message back unchanged, and if a filter is kept anywhere, it must preserve both thinking block types. You don't need to prune old thinking to save tokens either: the API filters prior turns' blocks itself and bills input only for the blocks it actually shows the model.

whyWrong.A: Toggling thinking mid-turn makes the API silently drop thinking for that request, so the error may go away while the reasoning behind the tool call is lost. It also fails with a 400 on models where thinking can't be turned off. It's a workaround, not a fix.
whyWrong.B: A 400 is a client error caused by the request's content. Retrying the same malformed history fails every time.
whyWrong.C: Prior turns' thinking may be omitted outside tool use, but the rule being violated concerns the latest assistant message in a tool-use turn, and this option still strips that one. Stripping more does not make it consistent.

questions.mindset: A 4xx means the request is wrong: fix the payload rather than retrying or switching features off.

questions.stem: An analyst-facing tool calls the Messages API through a hand-written HTTP client, without an official SDK. It sends non-streaming requests with a very large `max_tokens` to produce long reports, and users wait in the UI for the result. On the corporate network, some requests run for several minutes and then fail with no response from the API, while short requests succeed. What change is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Raise the client's read timeout to 30 minutes, so the client keeps waiting long enough for the full non-streaming response to arrive.
Lower `max_tokens` a lot so that every request finishes quickly, and accept that the longest reports will be shorter than they are today.
Switch these calls to the streaming Messages API so the connection carries data the whole time, and consider TCP keep-alive in the custom client.
Wrap each request in an automatic retry loop that resends it up to three times, so a dropped connection is recovered without the user noticing.

questions.explanation: The API docs warn against setting a large `max_tokens` without streaming or batches, because some networks drop idle connections, and a long non-streaming request can then fail with no response. Streaming keeps data flowing. TCP keep-alive also reduces idle drops for direct integrations, and the SDKs set it for you. The official SDKs also check that non-streaming requests aren't expected to exceed a 10-minute timeout. The Batches API fits jobs that can wait, but users here are waiting in the UI.

whyWrong.A: The connection is dropped by the network while it sits idle, not by the client timing out. A longer client timeout means users wait longer for the same failure.
whyWrong.B: Cutting `max_tokens` truncates the reports users need. It shrinks the symptom and gives up the requirement.
whyWrong.D: Each retry repeats the same long idle request on the same network, so it adds cost and wait time without fixing the cause.

questions.mindset: Match the transport to the workload: long generations should stream.

questions.stem: A back-office service gets occasional HTTP 500 `api_error` responses from the Claude API. Most of them clear on their own, but over two days a small set of requests has failed every time it was sent. The on-call engineer wants the service to handle these well and wants to escalate the persistent failures in a way Anthropic can investigate quickly. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Switch the service to the largest available model, because larger models give fewer internal server errors on hard prompts.
Retry 500 responses with exponential backoff, using the SDK's built-in retries or an equivalent policy, instead of failing on the first attempt.
Treat all 4xx and 5xx responses the same way and retry them in a tight loop until they succeed, so that no request is lost.
Ask the model to check its own output and resend the request whenever the response looks incomplete, wrong, or inconsistent in any way.
Log the `request-id` header (also returned as `request_id` in error bodies) and include those IDs when contacting support about the persistent failures.

questions.explanation: For a 500 `api_error`, the docs say to retry with exponential backoff and, if the error persists, contact support with the request ID. Every response has a `request-id` header, and error bodies repeat it as `request_id`. Logging it is what lets support trace the specific failing requests. The official SDKs already retry 5xx errors with backoff, twice by default.

whyWrong.A: Model size has nothing to do with internal server errors. This is the bigger-model distractor.
whyWrong.C: Most client errors (400, 401, 403, 404, 413) need the request fixed, not retried. The one retryable 4xx, 429, wants backoff that honors `retry-after`, and a tight loop without backoff makes any overload worse.
whyWrong.D: A 500 is an HTTP error with no usable response. Having the model check its output does nothing for transport failures and adds cost.

questions.mindset: Retry transient server errors with backoff, and bring request IDs when you escalate.

questions.stem: During a production outage, an SRE wants to use Claude Code to work through logs, metrics and cluster state to find the root cause. Today she pastes log fragments into the chat, and Claude's hypotheses keep missing context. The incident commander has one firm requirement: nothing Claude does during the investigation may change production state. Which TWO measures BEST meet both goals? Choose TWO.

options.text: Connect the team's observability and log platforms through MCP servers, so Claude can query real logs and metrics directly instead of working from pasted fragments.
Add a CLAUDE.md section titled 'Incident rules' telling Claude never to run mutating commands against production while an investigation is in progress.
Start the session in `bypassPermissions` mode so Claude can move quickly through diagnostics without stopping for approval prompts during the outage.
Give the session only read-only production credentials, such as a view-only cluster role and read-scoped observability tokens, so no command it attempts can change state.
Rely on plan mode for the whole investigation, since it guarantees that Claude cannot run any shell command until a plan is approved.

questions.explanation: There are two goals: better evidence and a hard guarantee of no changes. MCP connections to observability tools let Claude query real data instead of partial pastes. Read-only credentials enforce the no-change rule at the system boundary, so it holds even for a command spelled in a way no permission pattern expected. Deny or ask rules for destructive commands are a useful extra layer on top, but least-privilege credentials are the deterministic control.

whyWrong.B: An instruction guides Claude but enforces nothing. The incident commander's requirement needs a deterministic control.
whyWrong.C: Bypass mode removes the approval prompts the team relies on, which is the opposite of what the requirement needs.
whyWrong.E: Plan mode blocks file edits until a plan is approved, but shell commands can still run while planning (classifier-approved in auto mode, or prompted otherwise). It also ends when a plan is approved, so it isn't a guarantee.

questions.mindset: Give the agent real evidence, and enforce safety with least privilege rather than instructions.
